subject: physics

items.q: A rock sample contains unstable nuclei. Which statement best describes radioactive decay?
items.correct: An unstable nucleus gives out radiation at random as it changes to become more stable.
items.misconception: Each unstable nucleus gives out its radiation at a time that can be predicted.
items.why: Half-life is quoted as a definite number and decay graphs are smooth, so decay looks like clockwork. The definite half-life is a statistical result from an enormous number of nuclei. A single nucleus only has a chance of decaying in the next second.
items.random_wrong: A nucleus gives out radiation only after the rock has been heated strongly.

items.q: A teacher says that the activity of a source is falling. What does activity mean?
items.correct: The rate at which unstable nuclei in a source decay.
items.misconception: The number of decays a nearby detector records each second.
items.why: Both are quoted per second and both fall together, so the two numbers feel interchangeable. The detector only intercepts radiation that happens to travel towards it and be absorbed, so the count-rate is always lower than the activity.
items.random_wrong: The energy released by each decay in this source.

items.q: The activity of a source is given as 480 Bq. What does the becquerel measure?
items.correct: The number of decays that happen in a source each second.
items.misconception: The energy the radiation from a source gives out each second.
items.why: Radiation units are met together, and Bq is grouped with the units used for absorbed dose. The becquerel counts events: one becquerel is one decay each second. It says nothing about the energy carried.
items.random_wrong: The number of counts a Geiger-Muller tube records each minute.

items.q: A student monitors a source with a Geiger-Muller tube. What is the count-rate?
items.correct: The number of decays recorded each second by the detector.
items.misconception: The number of nuclei that decay in the whole source each second.
items.why: Both are quoted per second and both fall together, so the two numbers feel interchangeable. The detector only intercepts radiation that happens to travel towards it and be absorbed, so the count-rate is always lower than the activity.
items.random_wrong: The energy given to the Geiger-Muller tube by radiation each second.

items.q: Which list gives the types of nuclear radiation that an unstable nucleus may emit?
items.correct: Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons.
items.misconception: Alpha particles, beta particles, X-rays and neutrons.
items.why: It is listed alongside alpha and beta particles, so it is assumed to be a particle too. Gamma is part of the electromagnetic spectrum. It has no mass and no charge, which is why gamma emission changes neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and protons.

items.q: What is an alpha particle made of?
items.correct: Two neutrons and two protons, which is the same as a helium nucleus.
items.misconception: Two protons and two neutrons with two electrons in orbit around them.
items.why: The words 'helium nucleus' and the symbol ⁴₂He look like the helium already known from chemistry. Only the nucleus is emitted. There are no electrons in it, which is why an alpha particle carries a charge of +2.
items.random_wrong: A single fast electron that has been thrown out of the nucleus.

items.q: How do the properties of alpha radiation compare with those of beta and gamma?
items.correct: It ionises most strongly and is stopped by a sheet of paper.
items.misconception: It is the most penetrating radiation and travels furthest in air.
items.why: Being large and massive is read as being powerful, so the biggest particle is assumed to push furthest. Being large and highly charged makes alpha interact with almost every atom it meets, so it loses its energy within a few centimetres of air.
items.random_wrong: It is the least ionising but has the longest range in air.

items.q: What is a beta particle, and where does it come from?
items.correct: A high speed electron ejected as a neutron turns into a proton.
items.misconception: A high speed electron knocked out of one of the outer electron shells.
items.why: Electrons are taught as shell particles, so an emitted electron is assumed to be a shell electron. The electron is created in the nucleus at the instant a neutron changes into a proton. That is why the atomic number rises.
items.random_wrong: An electron that had already been stored inside the nucleus itself.

items.q: A beta source is placed near a detector and different absorbers are tried. Which description of beta radiation is correct?
items.correct: It is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and travels about a metre in air.
items.misconception: It is stopped by a sheet of paper and travels only a few centimetres.
items.why: Being large and massive is read as being powerful, so the biggest particle is assumed to push furthest. Being large and highly charged makes alpha interact with almost every atom it meets, so it loses its energy within a few centimetres of air.
items.random_wrong: It ionises more strongly than an alpha particle and is stopped by card.

items.q: What is a gamma ray?
items.correct: Electromagnetic radiation given out from the nucleus of an atom.
items.misconception: A heavy particle with no charge that is thrown out of the nucleus.
items.why: It is listed alongside alpha and beta particles, so it is assumed to be a particle too. Gamma is part of the electromagnetic spectrum. It has no mass and no charge, which is why gamma emission changes neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: Radiation given out when an electron moves between two shells.

items.q: Which statement about gamma radiation is correct?
items.correct: It is the least ionising radiation and the most penetrating one.
items.misconception: It is the most ionising radiation because it penetrates the furthest.
items.why: Penetration and ionising power are both treated as measures of how strong a radiation is, so they are assumed to rise together. They run in opposite directions. Gamma passes through matter precisely because it interacts with so few atoms on the way.
items.random_wrong: It is completely absorbed by a thin sheet of lead or thin concrete.

items.q: Some unstable nuclei emit a neutron. Which statement about this emission is correct?
items.correct: A neutron (n) is one of the nuclear radiations a nucleus emits.
items.misconception: A neutron cannot leave a nucleus, so this must really be beta decay.
items.why: Alpha, beta and gamma are drilled as 'the three radiations', so the fourth bullet is overlooked. The specification lists four possible emissions: alpha, beta, gamma and a neutron.
items.random_wrong: The neutron carries a negative charge out of the nucleus with it.

items.q: In a smoke alarm the radiation crosses a small gap in air and is absorbed when smoke enters the gap. Which source is best, and why?
items.correct: Alpha, because it ionises strongly and is absorbed over a short range in air.
items.misconception: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and always reaches the sensor.
items.why: 'Most penetrating' is treated as 'best' for every job, without asking what the device needs to detect. The alarm works because smoke absorbs the radiation crossing a small gap. Gamma would pass through the smoke and the reading would not change.
items.random_wrong: Beta, because it goes through smoke and is easy for a detector to see.

items.q: A paper mill measures the thickness of paper by detecting radiation that passes through it. Which source should be chosen?
items.correct: Beta, because the amount getting through changes as the thickness changes.
items.misconception: Alpha, because it ionises most strongly and gives the largest reading of all.
items.why: Strong ionisation is read as a strong reading, without asking whether any radiation reaches the detector at all. Paper stops alpha completely and barely affects gamma. Only beta is partly absorbed, so only beta gives a reading that varies with thickness.
items.random_wrong: Gamma, because it passes through the paper without being changed.

items.q: A tracer is injected into a patient and its progress is followed by a detector held outside the body. Which source is most suitable?
items.correct: A gamma emitter, because gamma passes out through the body tissue.
items.misconception: An alpha emitter, because alpha ionises most and is the easiest to detect.
items.why: Alpha is remembered as the most ionising, so it is assumed to make the clearest signal in every arrangement. Alpha would be absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue, so nothing would reach the detector and the patient would receive the whole dose.
items.random_wrong: An alpha emitter, because paper stops alpha so it is harmless inside.

items.q: In a nuclear equation, which symbol represents an alpha particle?
items.correct: The symbol ⁴₂He, which is a helium nucleus.
items.misconception: The symbol ²₄He, with the 2 written above the 4.
items.why: The two numbers are learned as a pair without linking each to what it counts, so their positions are swapped. The top number is always the mass number. An alpha particle has 4 nucleons and 2 protons, so it is ⁴₂He.
items.random_wrong: The symbol ⁰₋₁e, an electron from the nucleus.

items.q: Which symbol is used for a beta particle in a nuclear equation?
items.correct: ⁰₋₁e, so the mass number is 0 and the charge is −1.
items.misconception: ⁰₊₁e, so the mass number is 0 and charge is +1.
items.why: Beta decay is known to make the nucleus more positive, and the plus sign is attached to the beta particle itself. The beta particle is an electron, so its charge is −1 and its mass number is 0. It is the nucleus left behind whose charge rises.
items.random_wrong: ¹₋₁e, giving a mass number of 1 and charge −1.

items.q: A nucleus emits an alpha particle. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
items.correct: The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
items.misconception: The mass number falls by 2 and so does the atomic number.
items.why: Only the protons in the alpha particle are counted, and the two neutrons that also leave are forgotten. An alpha particle is two protons plus two neutrons, so four nucleons leave: mass number down 4, atomic number down 2.
items.random_wrong: The mass number falls by 4 but the atomic number does not.

items.q: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?
items.correct: The mass does not change but the charge increases by 1.
items.misconception: The mass falls by 1 and the charge of the nucleus increases by 1.
items.why: Something leaving is expected to reduce the mass, and the neutron becoming a proton is not tracked. The electron has a mass number of 0, and the neutron that vanished has been replaced by a proton, so the count of nucleons is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: The mass does not change and the charge of the nucleus falls by 1.

items.q: When a nuclear equation for alpha decay is balanced, which quantities must be equal on both sides?
items.correct: The total mass number and the total atomic number.
items.misconception: The number of protons only, as neutrons carry no charge.
items.why: Only the protons in the alpha particle are counted, and the two neutrons that also leave are forgotten. An alpha particle is two protons plus two neutrons, so four nucleons leave: mass number down 4, atomic number down 2.
items.random_wrong: The mass numbers only, as charge leaves with the alpha.

items.q: Carbon-14 decays by beta emission: ¹⁴₆C → ᴬZ N + ⁰₋₁e. Which values of A and Z balance this equation?
items.correct: A = 14 and Z = 7, since the charge rises as the mass stays the same.
items.misconception: A = 13 and Z = 7, since a particle has left the nucleus here.
items.why: Something leaving is expected to reduce the mass, and the neutron becoming a proton is not tracked. The electron has a mass number of 0, and the neutron that vanished has been replaced by a proton, so the count of nucleons is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: A = 14 and Z = 5, since a negative particle has been lost.

items.q: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?
items.correct: Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus is changed at all.
items.misconception: The mass number falls a little because energy has been carried off.
items.why: Alpha and beta decay both change the numbers, so gamma is assumed to change them as well. A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers in the nuclear symbol stay the same.
items.random_wrong: The charge increases by one but the mass number is the same.

items.q: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?
items.correct: It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.
items.misconception: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
items.why: Half-life is quoted as a definite number and decay graphs are smooth, so decay looks like clockwork. The definite half-life is a statistical result from an enormous number of nuclei. A single nucleus only has a chance of decaying in the next second.
items.random_wrong: The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.

items.q: The half-life of an isotope is 6 hours. What does this tell you about a sample of it?
items.correct: In 6 hours the count rate from the sample halves.
items.misconception: In 6 hours every nucleus in the sample will have decayed.
items.why: The word 'life' suggests a lifetime, so 'half-life' is read as a fraction of the time until the sample is finished. Half-life measures halving, not finishing. After each half-life whatever is left halves again, so there is always something left.
items.random_wrong: In 12 hours the sample will contain no unstable nuclei.

items.q: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?
items.correct: Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
items.misconception: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
items.why: Half-life is quoted as a definite number and decay graphs are smooth, so decay looks like clockwork. The definite half-life is a statistical result from an enormous number of nuclei. A single nucleus only has a chance of decaying in the next second.
items.random_wrong: Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.

items.q: The count rate from a source falls from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 24 minutes. What is the half-life?
items.correct: 8 minutes: three halvings take place
items.misconception: 24 minutes: only one halving takes place
items.why: The word 'life' suggests a lifetime, so 'half-life' is read as a fraction of the time until the sample is finished. Half-life measures halving, not finishing. After each half-life whatever is left halves again, so there is always something left.
items.random_wrong: 12 minutes: half of the total time

items.q: (HT only) The emission from a source is measured, and measured again after 4 half-lives have passed. What is the net decline, expressed as a ratio?
items.correct: 1 : 16, as the emission halves four times over
items.misconception: 1 : 4, as there are four half-lives in total here
items.why: The number of half-lives is used directly as the dividing factor instead of as a power of 2. Halving four times divides by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, so the ratio is 1 : 16.
items.random_wrong: 16 : 1, since the emission is now sixteen times less

items.q: A worker finds radioactive dust on their overalls. Which statement describes the situation correctly?
items.correct: This is contamination; the hazard is the decay of the dust.
items.misconception: This is contamination, but it is only a hazard if the dust can be seen.
items.why: Hazard is associated with contact, and contaminating dust is often invisible, so it is assumed to be harmless once out of sight. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms. Invisible dust on skin, clothes or food keeps decaying wherever it is.
items.random_wrong: This is irradiation, and the overalls have now become radioactive.

items.q: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?
items.correct: The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.
items.misconception: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
items.why: Radiation is pictured as a substance that soaks into things, like a dye or a smell. Radiation passes through or is absorbed, but leaves no radioactive atoms behind. Once the source is removed the object is safe.
items.random_wrong: The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.

items.q: Why is an alpha emitter more hazardous inside the body than outside it?
items.correct: Inside, its strong ionisation is absorbed by cells; outside, skin stops it.
items.misconception: It is never a hazard inside, because a sheet of paper is able to stop alpha.
items.why: The absorber table is memorised as a safety ranking, without asking where the source is. Inside the body there is no paper or skin in the way, and alpha's strong ionisation is all absorbed by nearby cells.
items.random_wrong: Gamma is worse inside the body, because it passes through everything.

items.q: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate surgical equipment. Which precaution is appropriate?
items.correct: Handle the source with tongs and store it in a lead-lined box.
items.misconception: None is needed, because irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
items.why: The safety of the irradiated object is confused with the safety of the people near the source. The object is safe, but the source itself keeps emitting. People are shielded from it, kept at a distance, and exposed for as short a time as possible.
items.random_wrong: Wear a paper mask, since paper is able to absorb gamma radiation.

items.q: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?
items.correct: So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
items.misconception: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
items.why: 'Review' is associated with approval by an authority or with public opinion. Peer review is checking by other scientists with the expertise to repeat the work and spot mistakes in it.
items.random_wrong: So that the government decides which findings should be believed.

items.q: Does nuclear radiation come from the electrons?
items.correct: No. It is emitted by the nucleus.
items.misconception: Radiation is given out when electrons move between energy levels closer to the nucleus.
items.why: Light emission by electrons changing energy level is taught elsewhere and is transferred to radioactivity. Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus. Nothing the electrons do can start it, stop it or alter its rate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How far does an alpha particle travel in air?
items.correct: Only a few centimetres.
items.misconception: Alpha travels several metres through air, as beta and gamma do.
items.why: All three are called radiation, so all three are assumed to reach across a room. Alpha ionises so strongly that it runs out of energy within a few centimetres. Beta travels about a metre and gamma travels much further.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does lead stop gamma radiation completely?
items.correct: No. Thick lead or concrete reduces gamma radiation, but some always gets through.
items.misconception: A thin sheet of lead absorbs gamma radiation completely, the way paper absorbs alpha.
items.why: The absorber table is memorised as 'paper, aluminium, lead' with the same word 'stopped' used for all three rows. Gamma is only reduced by an absorber. The thicker the lead, the smaller the count-rate, but it never reaches zero.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can heating a source change how fast it decays?
items.correct: No. The rate of decay is not affected by heating, pressure or chemical change.
items.misconception: Radioactive decay speeds up when the material is heated, as a chemical reaction does.
items.why: Every other rate met in science, from dissolving to reacting, depends on temperature. Decay is a nuclear process. Heating changes only the motion of the atoms, and cannot reach the nucleus.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the charge of the nucleus fall in beta decay?
items.correct: No. Beta decay causes the charge of the nucleus to increase by 1.
items.misconception: The atomic number falls by 1 because a negatively charged particle has been lost.
items.why: Losing a negative particle sounds like losing charge, and the minus sign in ⁰₋₁e reinforces it. Losing a negative charge leaves the nucleus more positive. A neutron has become a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a sample completely decayed after two half-lives?
items.correct: No. A quarter of the original nuclei are still undecayed.
items.misconception: Two half-lives means two lots of a half, which uses up the whole sample.
items.why: Halves are added rather than applied one after the other, so 50% + 50% is taken to be 100%. The second half-life halves what is left, not the original. After two half-lives a quarter remains, after three an eighth.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the half-life change as a sample decays?
items.correct: No. The half-life of an isotope stays the same however much of the sample is left.
items.misconception: The half-life gets shorter, or the decay speeds up, as fewer nuclei remain.
items.why: The count rate falls with time, which is read as the process changing rather than as fewer nuclei being available to decay. Each remaining nucleus always has the same chance of decaying in the next second, so the time to halve is always the same.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should a net decline be written 1 : 16 or 16 : 1?
items.correct: 1 : 16, comparing the final emission with the initial emission.
items.misconception: The ratio is written 16 : 1 because the activity has fallen sixteenfold.
items.why: The factor 16 is found correctly and then written first out of habit, without deciding which quantity each side stands for. A net decline compares what is left with what there was: final to initial. Sixteen times smaller is written 1 : 16.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which radiation is the greater hazard from a source inside the body?
items.correct: Alpha, because all of its strongly ionising energy is absorbed by the surrounding tissue.
items.misconception: Gamma is the greater hazard wherever the source is, because it goes through everything.
items.why: Gamma is the more dangerous source outside the body, and that ranking is applied without change to a source inside it. Gamma mostly passes straight out of the body without being absorbed. Alpha deposits all its energy in a small volume of tissue.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the nucleus store electrons ready to emit as beta particles?
items.correct: No. The electron is created as a neutron turns into a proton.
items.misconception: The nucleus contains electrons already, and beta decay simply lets one escape.
items.why: 'Ejected from the nucleus' is read as 'was already sitting in the nucleus'. There are no electrons in a nucleus. The beta particle comes into existence at the moment a neutron changes into a proton.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do nuclei emit protons as one of the types of nuclear radiation?
items.correct: The specification lists alpha, beta, gamma and neutrons. A lone proton is not one of them.
items.misconception: Since a nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, it emits protons as a common form of radiation.
items.why: Neutron emission is on the list, so the other nucleon is assumed to be emitted too. Protons leave only bound up in an alpha particle, which is two protons and two neutrons together.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many times does the emission halve in 4 half-lives?
items.correct: Four times, giving a factor of 16.
items.misconception: Four half-lives means the 2 in halving multiplied by the 4, giving a factor of 8.
items.why: The 2 in 'halving' and the 4 in 'four half-lives' are combined by multiplying instead of using 2 to the power 4. Each half-life multiplies the emission by 1/2, so four of them give 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2, which is 1/16.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are studies of radiation effects published?
items.correct: So the findings can be checked by other scientists through peer review.
items.misconception: Findings are published so the researchers get credit and further funding for their work.
items.why: Publication is visible as a reward for scientists, so its role in checking the science is overlooked. Credit may follow, but the scientific purpose is that others can examine, repeat and challenge the findings before they are relied on.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
